bridges.mechanism: A sustained decline in crude flow through Gulf chokepoints increases competition for alternative supplies and discrete energy deals, which exacerbates bilateral frictions (notably between China and India) over access and pricing.

A sustained reduction in physical crude flows signals tighter energy availability, prompting markets to raise expected future policy rates as they price a higher probability of central‑bank tightening to counter energy‑driven inflationary pressure.

A drop in chokepoint throughput physically delays or prevents sea shipments of weapons, ammunition and heavy equipment bound for Europe, lowering the volume and punctuality of material aid reaching Ukrainian recipients.

A drop in chokepoint throughput produces immediate container and specialized-cargo backlogs that delay deliveries of GPUs, servers and spare parts, lengthening model-training cycles and slowing near-term AI capability improvements.

A rise in shipping risk premiums directly raises transport and insurance costs and delivery uncertainty for China-India and wider BRICS trade, prompting firms to cut volumes and delay cross-border investment decisions.
Higher shipping risk premiums raise delivered transport costs and reduce effective arbitrage between crude hubs, tightening available supply to end markets and pushing spot oil prices up.
Higher insurance and surcharge costs raise the landed price and lead-times for finished AI products and edge hardware, causing firms to delay product launches or scale back commercial rollouts.
Escalating Gulf conflict drives near‑term global risk‑off flows into core sovereign debt (e.g., US Treasuries, German bunds), boosting demand for safe assets and pushing long‑term yields down.

A surge in hostile incidents around Gulf chokepoints forces Western and regional militaries to reassign ISR and strike UAS assets to maritime and littoral protection tasks, reducing sortie rates available for operations over Ukraine.

Escalating Iran–Gulf hostilities prompt allied governments to accelerate national-security reviews and enact export controls, investment screens, and targeted AI policy measures, increasing regulatory activity.
Faster mobilization and ramp‑up of alternative supplies and rerouting restores displaced barrels to the market, relieving short‑term tightness and lowering crude prices.

Faster mobilization of alternative routing and sourcing (airlift, longer sea routes, alternative ports) offsets Gulf disruptions and preserves/accelerates the flow of weapons and materiel into the Ukraine theatre.

Frequent cross‑border strikes that disrupt global food and energy transit create immediate supply‑security pressures that drive BRICS members into ad hoc meetings and communiqués to align export controls, shipping routes and contingency policies.
An uptick in cross‑border strikes that threaten production, pipelines, terminals or shipping routes raises the market's perceived risk of supply disruptions, causing crude oil prices to rise.

High-volume combat use of armed UAS in Ukraine accelerates tactical diffusion and market supply of proven drone kits and tactics to regional actors, enabling more frequent and effective strikes on shipping and energy infrastructure in the Gulf, raising incident frequency and severity.

Higher sortie rates and deployment of semi‑autonomous drones produce more failure modes, adversarial exploitation, and misidentification events that increase the frequency of reported and unreported AI safety and misuse incidents.

Sustained increases in Western weapons and aid to Ukraine prompt Russia to reroute energy, commodity exports and investment partnerships toward China and India to replace lost Western markets, directly raising trade and investment flows between Russia and BRICS partners.

Larger Western arms and assistance packages increase the likelihood and severity of financial restrictions on Russia, incentivizing BRICS members to expand alternative payment channels, currency-swap arrangements and bilateral settlement mechanisms to preserve commerce with Russia.

Sustained high-volume weapons and aid flows signal a protracted conflict, raising a geopolitical risk premium on sovereign debt and pushing up long-term government bond yields as investors demand higher compensation.

Large, sustained flows of weapons, sensors, and operational data into the theatre accelerate R&D and field testing by allied contractors and researchers, speeding improvements in core AI models and specialist systems.

A growing fiscal burden on external supporters increases expected future government borrowing and issuance to fund military and humanitarian assistance, directly lifting long-term sovereign yields through higher supply and weaker fiscal metrics.

Sustained fiscal and material strain on Western and allied backers forces reallocation and reduced availability of naval patrols, escorts and maintenance funding for Gulf deployments, lowering the effective operational throughput and safe-transit capacity of chokepoints.

A higher measured risk that the Russia–Ukraine conflict will escalate or spill over raises strategic uncertainty regionally, prompting India and China (and other BRICS pairs) to increase military readiness and diplomatic distrust, thereby elevating bilateral tensions.

Higher risk of geographic or institutional spillover drives wider credit spreads, higher volatility and reduced risk appetite, tightening the composite financial conditions indicator as funding costs and constraints increase.

An elevated systemic probability of geographic or institutional spillover from the Ukraine conflict increases insurers' and charterers' perceived exposure for tanker transits through Gulf chokepoints, pushing up war‑risk and security-related transport premiums almost immediately.

Rising risk that the conflict will spill over or draw in external actors prompts US/allied policymakers to rapidly expand export controls, emergency vetting, and other AI governance measures to limit dual‑use transfers and hurry legislative responses.
Stronger bloc cohesion enables rapid coordinated liquidity provision, swap lines and policy signalling that reduce risk premia and credit strain, easing global financial conditions.

Greater cohesion within BRICS (notably between China and Russia) provides political cover and reduces perceived international costs for riskier Russian operations, increasing the systemic probability of geographic or institutional spillover from the Ukraine theatre.
Escalating China–India bilateral tensions trigger risk‑off behavior, widen EM and corporate spreads and increase volatility, thereby tightening overall financial conditions.

Rising China–India bilateral tensions prompt higher naval deployments, patrols and security cooperation with regional partners in the Indian Ocean, elevating the frequency of risky encounters, interdictions or shadowing that can escalate into hostile incidents affecting Gulf shipping and infrastructure linked to Iran.

Escalating China–India bilateral tensions increase state and proxy cyber operations (esp. data poisoning, supply-chain attacks) that directly raise the frequency of AI safety and misuse incidents affecting systems used by US-allied actors.

Deeper China–India financial linkages and payment arrangements shorten settlement friction and enable faster payments to alternative suppliers and shipowners, increasing the speed and volume at which replacement crude and rerouted shipments can be mobilized after a disruption.

Deeper BRICS financial linkages and alternative payment rails reduce sanctions frictions and allow Russia and its suppliers to settle purchases and logistics more easily, increasing the volume and regularity of arms and materiel reaching conflict actors.
A surge in bilateral trade and investment activity raises short-term transport and industrial fuel demand (and logistic bottlenecks), directly increasing crude oil demand and lifting oil prices.

An increase in China–India trade and energy procurement directly raises tanker liftings from Persian Gulf exporters, physically increasing the barrels per day transiting regional chokepoints (e.g., Strait of Hormuz).

An uptick in China–BRICS trade and investment — including relaxed export controls or increased shipments of UAS components and dual‑use electronics from China — directly supplies Russia with parts and finished drones, enabling higher sortie rates in the theatre.

A sustained increase in China–India trade and investment creates larger integrated markets and revenue streams for China/India-based AI firms, forcing US-allied firms to accelerate productization and market rollouts to defend market share.

Stronger China–India policy coordination to provide diplomatic protection, coordinated state-backed insurance or organized convoy/escort arrangements reduces insurers' perceived exposure and thus lowers the incremental shipping risk premium on Gulf-to-Asia routes.

Stronger, coordinated BRICS diplomacy that blocks or weakens sanctions enforcement and export controls prolongs the conflict by sustaining Russian sustainment pathways, forcing external supporters to maintain or raise military and humanitarian aid budgets and thus increasing their fiscal burden.

Stronger coordinated BRICS policy moves (e.g., harmonized data, export or standard-setting actions) produce concrete cross-border policy pressure that prompts US-allied governments to increase legislative and regulatory activity to protect domestic firms and maintain tech controls.

Rising global inflation expectations increase domestic political and policy pressure on BRICS members to prioritize national inflation control and protective measures, reducing their willingness and bandwidth to negotiate and implement coordinated multilateral policies.

Rising inflation expectations prompt insurers and P&I clubs to raise premiums and add surcharges to cover anticipated higher claims and replacement costs, increasing the per-unit shipping risk premium for oil shipments through the Gulf.

An increase in crude oil prices raises shipping, input and energy costs for exporters and importers, directly depressing bilateral trade volumes and raising transaction costs for China–India commercial flows and broader BRICS trade.

Sustained higher oil prices raise the value of rents and sanction-leverage for Gulf producers and non-state actors, enabling greater funding and incentive to conduct maritime harassment or attacks on shipping to extract concessions or signal power, thereby increasing hostile incidents.

Higher crude prices raise energy-exporting states' fiscal and FX receipts (notably Russia), enabling larger direct procurement and stockpiling of munitions and spare parts and reducing the need to pause purchases, thereby increasing the volume of weapons and material flowing into the conflict.

Rising oil prices increase import bills and inflation for energy‑importing donor states, tightening their budgets and making each tranche of military and humanitarian assistance a larger fiscal burden for external supporters.

A rise in advanced-economy long-term government yields re-prices global safe assets and triggers rapid portfolio reallocation away from emerging-market exposures, causing immediate capital outflows and a drop in cross-border financing and FDI that reduces trade and investment flows to China and India.

A sustained rise in long-term sovereign yields raises the effective cost of financing for donor governments and defense procurement, prompting budgetary re‑prioritization or delay of large transfers and thereby reducing the near‑term volume and tempo of weapons and aid deliveries.

Rising long-term sovereign yields raise the discount rate and depress startup valuations and exit prospects, reducing VC and corporate M&A funding that directly finances productization and market rollouts of AI, slowing commercialization.

Higher expected policy rates increase borrowing and opportunity costs for firms and cloud/compute purchasers, causing delays or scale-backs of large compute-intensive training runs and multi-quarter R&D projects that drive core AI capability improvements.

Tighter global financial conditions (wider spreads, higher volatility, reduced credit availability) prompt banks and asset managers to de-risk and cut cross-border lending and wholesale funding, directly shrinking the depth of financial linkages and coordination among BRICS, including China and India.

Tighter financial conditions increase shipping and trade finance costs and constrain working capital for carriers and terminals, leading to stretched schedules, deferred sailings and maintenance, and thus a measurable reduction in effective throughput at major chokepoints.

Tighter financial conditions (higher spreads, reduced credit) constrain defense contractors' and frontline units' ability to purchase parts, finance maintenance, and sustain fuel/logistics chains, which lowers sortie rates and active operational density of drones.

Tighter financial conditions force firms to prioritize near-term revenue and cut discretionary spending, producing immediate reductions in budgets for internal safety teams, red‑teaming, audits, and rollout controls, lowering operational safety adoption.

Rapid increases in US‑allied AI capabilities spur deeper India‑US security and technology collaboration (shared procurement, joint R&D and intelligence exchanges), which China interprets as a shifting balance and responds with military/diplomatic measures that elevate China–India bilateral tensions.

Faster core AI capability improvements accelerate allied and proxy deployment of improved ISR, autonomous maritime systems, and advanced cyber/targeting tools, lowering thresholds and increasing the frequency and precision of hostile incidents in Gulf chokepoints.

Faster core AI capability improvements enable more capable autonomous navigation, targeting, and swarm coordination that operators rapidly integrate into UAS fleets, increasing sortie rates and on‑front operational density.

A surge in commercialization by US‑allied AI firms squeezes market space for BRICS incumbents and creates coordinated competitive pressures, prompting BRICS governments to align industrial policy, align regulatory responses and negotiate joint measures to protect or subsidize domestic AI sectors.

A rapid surge in allied commercial rollouts of advanced AI drives near-term demand for cloud compute, semiconductors and higher-margin digital services and consumption, lifting services prices and market inflation breakevens.

Accelerated commercialization of dual‑use AI and sensing tech lowers acquisition costs and shortens procurement timelines for militias and external suppliers, increasing the volume and regularity of matériel and enabling more frequent aid shipments.
Clustered or high-profile AI safety/security incidents provoke investor risk-aversion and sectoral equity sell-offs and widen corporate credit spreads, tightening overall financial conditions.

An uptick in AI safety and misuse incidents (e.g., navigation-autopilot failures, port automation errors, or spoofing of AIS/GPS systems) causes collisions, groundings and temporary port/strait closures that directly reduce throughput capacity at Gulf chokepoints.

An increase in AI‑related safety or misuse incidents (misattributed strikes, false alarms, cyber surprises) raises the probability of miscalculation and reactive measures that expand the conflict beyond the immediate theatre.

Heightened US‑allied regulatory activity (export controls and extraterritorial licensing on AI hardware, cloud services and dual‑use software) directly restricts BRICS firms' and investors' access to key inputs and markets, reducing cross‑border trade and investment volumes between BRICS members and external (US/allied) partners.

A marked increase in allied regulatory intervention on AI raises expected long-run drag on productivity and tech-sector growth, reducing the term premium and putting downward pressure on long-term government yields.

Heightened allied regulatory activity (export controls on AI models, compute and dual‑use software) reduces Iran's and its proxies' access to advanced AI-enabled targeting and autonomous strike components, degrading their capacity to sustain or escalate attacks on shipping and infrastructure.

Higher uptake of deployment‑level safety practices (geofencing, robust human‑in‑loop checks, red‑teaming) directly reduces navigation/targeting failures and errant engagements that would otherwise produce unintended cross‑border strikes.

Crude oil physical flow rate
nodes.description: Rate of crude oil physically transported through the global supply network measured in barrels per day.

nodes.label: Refined fuel flow rate
nodes.description: Rate of movement of refined petroleum products (diesel, gasoline, jet fuel) through refining and distribution channels measured in barrels per day.

nodes.label: Maritime chokepoint operational capacity
nodes.description: Functional throughput capacity of major maritime transit chokepoints measured in equivalent barrels per day.

nodes.label: Maritime transit rate
nodes.description: Number of vessel transits or oil shipments passing through key sea routes per unit time.

nodes.label: Tanker availability
nodes.description: Amount of deployable tanker cargo capacity available for oil transport measured in barrels.

nodes.label: Shipping risk premium
nodes.description: Additional per‑unit transport cost reflecting perceived security and insurance risk for maritime oil shipments.

nodes.label: Oil market price level
nodes.description: prevailing market price level of crude oil benchmarks measured in dollars per barrel.

nodes.label: Price volatility level
nodes.description: Magnitude of short‑term fluctuations in crude and refined fuel prices, measured as realized or implied volatility.

nodes.label: Total oil inventories
nodes.description: Aggregate stocks of crude and refined products held across commercial and strategic storage measured in barrels.

nodes.label: Refinery utilization rate
nodes.description: Share of global refining capacity currently operational, expressed as a percentage of nameplate capacity.

nodes.label: Pipeline operational capacity
nodes.description: Aggregate throughput capacity of major oil pipelines measured in barrels per day.

nodes.label: Conflict intensity
nodes.description: Frequency and severity of hostile incidents and military actions that affect energy infrastructure and shipping safety.

nodes.label: Sanctions restriction intensity
nodes.description: Degree and scope of legal and regulatory restrictions on energy transactions, logistics, and financing.

nodes.label: Diplomatic engagement level
nodes.description: Level of active diplomatic negotiation, mediation, and multilateral coordination aimed at de‑escalation and reopening routes.

nodes.label: Alternative supply response rate
nodes.description: Rate at which alternative supply sources and rerouting adjustments are mobilized to replace disrupted flows, measured in barrels per day per time unit.

nodes.label: Fuel distribution delay
nodes.description: Average delay in delivery times for refined fuels from refineries to end markets due to logistical disruptions, measured in days.

Escalation in the Russia–Ukraine war: drones, cross‑border strikes, and Western strain
Conflict intensity
nodes.description: Measures the overall kinetic tempo and severity of military operations across the theatre (rates of strikes, battles, and casualties).

nodes.label: Cross‑border strike rate
nodes.description: Measures the frequency and geographic reach of armed strikes that cross recognized borders or buffer zones.

nodes.label: Drone operational density
nodes.description: Measures the active presence and sortie rate of unmanned aerial systems used in offensive and reconnaissance roles within the conflict environment.

nodes.label: Long‑range precision capability
nodes.description: Measures the availability and effectiveness of weapons systems capable of striking distant targets with precision (range, accuracy, reliability).

nodes.label: Weapons and aid flow
nodes.description: Measures the volume and regularity of material support flows (weapons, ammunition, logistical aid, and funding) into conflict actors.

nodes.label: Defense support budget burden
nodes.description: Measures the fiscal strain placed on external supporters by sustained military and humanitarian assistance commitments.

nodes.label: Alliance cohesion
nodes.description: Measures the degree of political alignment, policy coordination, and mutual commitment among allied actors responding to the conflict.

nodes.label: Airspace control effectiveness
nodes.description: Measures the capability to detect, intercept, and deny hostile aerial systems and incursions over contested and border airspace.

nodes.label: Civilian infrastructure vulnerability
nodes.description: Measures the susceptibility of critical civilian assets (energy, transport, communications, water) to disruption or damage from attacks.

nodes.label: Displaced population flow
nodes.description: Measures the rate and direction of civilian population movements caused by insecurity, destruction, or loss of services.

nodes.label: Military‑technical adaptation rate
nodes.description: Measures the speed and magnitude of technological and organizational changes in military production and tactics in response to battlefield demands.

nodes.label: Sanction pressure level
nodes.description: Measures the aggregate economic and financial pressure applied through restrictive measures and their effective targeting intensity.

nodes.label: External public support
nodes.description: Measures popular political backing in states providing support, including tolerance for costs, casualties, and long‑term assistance.

nodes.label: Retaliation likelihood
nodes.description: Measures the propensity that an attack will trigger timely and escalatory counteractions by the targeted party.

nodes.label: Border security readiness
nodes.description: Measures the operational preparedness of forces and systems tasked with monitoring and defending land and transit borders.

nodes.label: Escalation and spillover risk
nodes.description: Measures the systemic probability that conflict dynamics will extend geographically or institutionally beyond the current theatre.

Greater US intelligence role in negotiations
BRICS summit: Strategic pivot and unity under stress
Bloc cohesion strength
nodes.description: The overall degree of mutual alignment, trust and coordinated action among member actors within the bloc.

nodes.label: Bilateral tension level
nodes.description: The aggregated intensity of bilateral political, territorial and diplomatic frictions between pairs of member actors.

nodes.label: Diplomatic engagement intensity
nodes.description: The rate and frequency of formal and informal diplomatic interactions, summit meetings and high-level talks among member actors.

nodes.label: Financial integration depth
nodes.description: The extent of cross-border financial linkages, coordination of finance policy and shared financial instruments among members.

nodes.label: Trade and investment flow
nodes.description: The volume and velocity of goods, services and capital transfers between member actors and with external partners.

nodes.label: External conflict pressure
nodes.description: The degree to which external armed conflicts and regional wars exert disruptive influence on the bloc's politics and cooperation.

nodes.label: Sanctions and restrictions pressure
nodes.description: The level and impact of external economic sanctions, trade restrictions and countermeasures affecting member actors.

nodes.label: Strategic hedging activity
nodes.description: The rate at which member actors diversify partnerships, create alternative economic linkages and pursue nonaligned options to reduce dependence.

nodes.label: Institutional influence capacity
nodes.description: The capacity of the bloc collectively to propose, shape or reform international institutional norms, rules and governance structures.

nodes.label: Resource dependency concentration
nodes.description: The concentration and criticality of key commodity and resource supply relationships among members and vis-à-vis external suppliers.

nodes.label: Market access openness
nodes.description: The degree to which members allow reciprocal trade and investment access, including tariff, non-tariff and regulatory barriers.

nodes.label: Cross-border payment linkage extent
nodes.description: The breadth and technical interoperability of cross-border payment systems, currency settlement arrangements and digital payment links among members.

nodes.label: Geopolitical polarization perception
nodes.description: The collective perception of alignment pressure between competing global power blocs and the degree members feel forced to choose sides.

nodes.label: Policy coordination strength
nodes.description: The effectiveness with which member actors negotiate, agree and implement joint policy declarations, communiqués and coordinated actions.

nodes.label: Infrastructure investment flow
nodes.description: The rate of cross-border capital commitments and executed projects for physical and digital infrastructure cooperation among members.

Bond selloff from sticky inflation and oil-driven rate fears
Headline inflation rate
nodes.description: The measured overall consumer price inflation rate including volatile items such as energy and food.

nodes.label: Core inflation rate
nodes.description: Consumer price inflation excluding volatile components, representing underlying inflation momentum.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: The market and public's expected future inflation path over relevant horizons.

nodes.label: Oil price level
nodes.description: The prevailing market price level for crude oil as a broad energy-price indicator.

nodes.label: Oil price volatility
nodes.description: The magnitude and frequency of short-term fluctuations in oil prices.

nodes.label: Long-term government bond yield
nodes.description: The prevailing market yield on long-dated sovereign bonds representing the cost of long-term government borrowing.

nodes.label: Term premium level
nodes.description: The component of long-term yields that compensates investors for interest-rate and reinvestment risk over the term.

nodes.label: Short-term policy rate
nodes.description: The current short-term policy interest rate set by monetary authorities that anchors overnight borrowing costs.

nodes.label: Policy rate expectations
nodes.description: The market-implied expected future path of short-term policy rates over coming policy cycles.

nodes.label: Market intervention intensity
nodes.description: The rate and scale of active market-support operations (e.g., asset purchases or buybacks) implemented to influence market prices.

nodes.label: Bond market liquidity
nodes.description: The ease, depth and breadth with which bonds can be transacted without large price impact.

nodes.label: Financial conditions
nodes.description: A composite measure of overall financial tightness including rates, spreads, credit availability and volatility.

nodes.label: Credit spread level
nodes.description: The average difference between corporate borrowing yields and sovereign yields reflecting credit risk premia.

nodes.label: Equity market valuation
nodes.description: The prevailing valuation metric of equity markets (e.g., aggregate price-to-earnings) reflecting price relative to fundamentals.

nodes.label: Exchange rate level
nodes.description: The prevailing value of the currency exchange rate relevant to the system (e.g., broad trade-weighted or a major bilateral rate).

nodes.label: Real growth expectations
nodes.description: The expected path of real economic activity or GDP growth over the medium term.

nodes.label: AI safety backlash amid rapid commercial and geopolitical race
AI capability growth rate
nodes.description: The rate at which core AI model capabilities (performance, generality, and autonomy) are improving over time.

nodes.label: Commercialization pace of AI
nodes.description: The speed and intensity with which advanced AI capabilities are packaged, productized, and deployed into commercial services and products.

nodes.label: Capital flow into AI
nodes.description: The volume and velocity of financial investment (VC, equity, debt) directed to AI development and deployment per unit time.

nodes.label: AI talent mobility
nodes.description: The rate at which skilled AI researchers and engineers move between organizations, sectors, and geographies.

nodes.label: Model diffusion and distribution
nodes.description: The rate at which trained models, weights, architectures, and related IP spread across actors and platforms.

nodes.label: Training data transfer volume
nodes.description: The amount and cross-border movement of data and query logs used for training and fine-tuning AI systems per unit time.

nodes.label: Safety and misuse incident frequency
nodes.description: The frequency of reported and unreported incidents in which AI systems cause harm, are misused, or produce security breaches.

nodes.label: Incident amplification feedback strength
nodes.description: The strength of the causal feedback from incidents to amplified responses (researcher alerts, media coverage, political pressure, market moves).

nodes.label: Researcher safety alarm level
nodes.description: The aggregated intensity and prevalence of public and private safety warnings, calls for slowdowns, and advocacy from the technical community.

nodes.label: Regulatory and policy activity
nodes.description: The level of legislative, regulatory, and enforcement activity focused on AI governance and controls.

nodes.label: Governance and oversight capacity
nodes.description: The capability of public institutions and oversight mechanisms to design, implement, and enforce effective AI rules and safeguards.

nodes.label: Operational safety adoption
nodes.description: The degree to which organizations have implemented internal safety processes, auditing, red-teaming, and deployment controls for AI systems.

nodes.label: Public trust and social acceptance
nodes.description: The overall level of societal trust, acceptance, and confidence in AI technologies and their deployment in everyday contexts.

nodes.label: Market valuation and financing pressure
nodes.description: The degree to which markets, investors, and capital markets reward or punish AI firms based on perceived growth, safety, and regulatory risk.

nodes.label: Security and military exploitation risk
nodes.description: The likelihood and severity that AI capabilities will be repurposed for offensive cyber, espionage, or weaponization by non-civilian actors.

An increase in crude oil prices raises shipping, input and energy costs for exporters and importers, directly depressing bilateral trade volumes and raising transaction costs for China–India commercial flows and broader BRICS trade.

Sustained higher oil prices raise the value of rents and sanction-leverage for Gulf producers and non-state actors, enabling greater funding and incentive to conduct maritime harassment or attacks on shipping to extract concessions or signal power, thereby increasing hostile incidents.

Higher crude prices raise energy-exporting states' fiscal and FX receipts (notably Russia), enabling larger direct procurement and stockpiling of munitions and spare parts and reducing the need to pause purchases, thereby increasing the volume of weapons and material flowing into the conflict.

Rising oil prices increase import bills and inflation for energy‑importing donor states, tightening their budgets and making each tranche of military and humanitarian assistance a larger fiscal burden for external supporters.

A rise in advanced-economy long-term government yields re-prices global safe assets and triggers rapid portfolio reallocation away from emerging-market exposures, causing immediate capital outflows and a drop in cross-border financing and FDI that reduces trade and investment flows to China and India.

A sustained rise in long-term sovereign yields raises the effective cost of financing for donor governments and defense procurement, prompting budgetary re‑prioritization or delay of large transfers and thereby reducing the near‑term volume and tempo of weapons and aid deliveries.

Rising long-term sovereign yields raise the discount rate and depress startup valuations and exit prospects, reducing VC and corporate M&A funding that directly finances productization and market rollouts of AI, slowing commercialization.

Higher expected policy rates increase borrowing and opportunity costs for firms and cloud/compute purchasers, causing delays or scale-backs of large compute-intensive training runs and multi-quarter R&D projects that drive core AI capability improvements.

Tighter global financial conditions (wider spreads, higher volatility, reduced credit availability) prompt banks and asset managers to de-risk and cut cross-border lending and wholesale funding, directly shrinking the depth of financial linkages and coordination among BRICS, including China and India.

Tighter financial conditions increase shipping and trade finance costs and constrain working capital for carriers and terminals, leading to stretched schedules, deferred sailings and maintenance, and thus a measurable reduction in effective throughput at major chokepoints.

Tighter financial conditions (higher spreads, reduced credit) constrain defense contractors' and frontline units' ability to purchase parts, finance maintenance, and sustain fuel/logistics chains, which lowers sortie rates and active operational density of drones.

Tighter financial conditions force firms to prioritize near-term revenue and cut discretionary spending, producing immediate reductions in budgets for internal safety teams, red‑teaming, audits, and rollout controls, lowering operational safety adoption.

Rapid increases in US‑allied AI capabilities spur deeper India‑US security and technology collaboration (shared procurement, joint R&D and intelligence exchanges), which China interprets as a shifting balance and responds with military/diplomatic measures that elevate China–India bilateral tensions.

Faster core AI capability improvements accelerate allied and proxy deployment of improved ISR, autonomous maritime systems, and advanced cyber/targeting tools, lowering thresholds and increasing the frequency and precision of hostile incidents in Gulf chokepoints.

Faster core AI capability improvements enable more capable autonomous navigation, targeting, and swarm coordination that operators rapidly integrate into UAS fleets, increasing sortie rates and on‑front operational density.

A surge in commercialization by US‑allied AI firms squeezes market space for BRICS incumbents and creates coordinated competitive pressures, prompting BRICS governments to align industrial policy, align regulatory responses and negotiate joint measures to protect or subsidize domestic AI sectors.

A rapid surge in allied commercial rollouts of advanced AI drives near-term demand for cloud compute, semiconductors and higher-margin digital services and consumption, lifting services prices and market inflation breakevens.

Accelerated commercialization of dual‑use AI and sensing tech lowers acquisition costs and shortens procurement timelines for militias and external suppliers, increasing the volume and regularity of matériel and enabling more frequent aid shipments.
Clustered or high-profile AI safety/security incidents provoke investor risk-aversion and sectoral equity sell-offs and widen corporate credit spreads, tightening overall financial conditions.

An uptick in AI safety and misuse incidents (e.g., navigation-autopilot failures, port automation errors, or spoofing of AIS/GPS systems) causes collisions, groundings and temporary port/strait closures that directly reduce throughput capacity at Gulf chokepoints.

An increase in AI‑related safety or misuse incidents (misattributed strikes, false alarms, cyber surprises) raises the probability of miscalculation and reactive measures that expand the conflict beyond the immediate theatre.

Heightened US‑allied regulatory activity (export controls and extraterritorial licensing on AI hardware, cloud services and dual‑use software) directly restricts BRICS firms' and investors' access to key inputs and markets, reducing cross‑border trade and investment volumes between BRICS members and external (US/allied) partners.

A marked increase in allied regulatory intervention on AI raises expected long-run drag on productivity and tech-sector growth, reducing the term premium and putting downward pressure on long-term government yields.

Heightened allied regulatory activity (export controls on AI models, compute and dual‑use software) reduces Iran's and its proxies' access to advanced AI-enabled targeting and autonomous strike components, degrading their capacity to sustain or escalate attacks on shipping and infrastructure.

Higher uptake of deployment‑level safety practices (geofencing, robust human‑in‑loop checks, red‑teaming) directly reduces navigation/targeting failures and errant engagements that would otherwise produce unintended cross‑border strikes.
